sentence: The NHS describes non-sedating antihistamines such as cetirizine as less likely to cause drowsiness than sedating ones such as chlorphenamine.
note: NHS pages place cetirizine as less likely than sedating antihistamines such as chlorphenamine (Piriton) to cause sleepiness (summary of Antihistamines/cetirizine pages).

sentence: Antihistamines block histamine, the chemical that triggers itching, sneezing and watery eyes during an allergic reaction.
note: NHS: cetirizine blocks the effects of histamine, which triggers allergy symptoms such as itching, sneezing, watery eyes.

sentence: Cetirizine, loratadine and fexofenadine are called non-sedating, while chlorphenamine (Piriton) is a sedating antihistamine.
note: Cambridge University Hospitals leaflet lists these as non-sedating; NHS says chlorphenamine is a sedating antihistamine.

sentence: Non-sedating does not mean never drowsy: the NHS says some people still find cetirizine sedating, and it advises care with driving and alcohol.
note: NHS cetirizine side effects: sleepiness most common; some find it sedating; not to drive or ride a bike if sleepy; best not to drink alcohol.

sentence: The NHS says chlorphenamine can be taken in pregnancy and a non-drowsy antihistamine such as loratadine may be suggested instead.
note: NHS: can be taken in pregnancy, no good evidence of harm to baby, can cause drowsiness; doctor or pharmacist may suggest a non-drowsy antihistamine such as loratadine.

sentence: A pharmacist or GP can advise on choosing an antihistamine; NHS 111 is for urgent advice, and 999 is for signs of a serious allergic reaction.
note: NHS chlorphenamine side effects page: contact doctor or NHS 111 for some effects; call 999 for signs of serious allergic reaction.

sentence: Antihistamines are medicines that block the effects of histamine.
note: NHS: cetirizine works by blocking the effects of histamine.

sentence: Histamine is a chemical that the body makes when it meets something it is allergic to, such as pollen or animal fur.
note: NHS cetirizine page: on contact with something allergic to (pollen, animal fur) the body produces histamine. Page attribution blended.

sentence: It is what sets off allergy symptoms such as itching, sneezing and watery eyes.
note: Search summary of NHS antihistamines/cetirizine pages: histamine triggers itching, sneezing, watery eyes.

sentence: People mostly use them for allergy problems such as hay fever.
note: NHS pages on cetirizine and antihistamines concern hay fever and allergy symptom relief; the summary notes people with hay fever generally buy them over the counter.

sentence: Antihistamines are often sorted into two groups, called sedating and non-sedating.
note: Cambridge University Hospitals leaflet is titled for non-sedating tablets and contrasts them with sedating ones; NHS antihistamines page covers both.

sentence: Sedating means more likely to cause sleepiness, and non-sedating means less likely.
note: CUH leaflet: non-sedating usually do not cause drowsiness; sedating carry more risk of drowsiness.

sentence: A hospital leaflet from Cambridge University Hospitals names cetirizine, loratadine and fexofenadine as non-sedating tablets that usually do not cause drowsiness, so they can be used in the daytime.
note: CUH leaflet: non-sedating tablets such as cetirizine, loratadine, fexofenadine usually do not cause drowsiness so can be taken during the day.

sentence: Chlorphenamine, which is sold as Piriton, is a sedating antihistamine.
note: NHS side effects page: chlorphenamine is a drowsy (sedating) antihistamine.

sentence: The NHS groups it with other sedating antihistamines such as cinnarizine and promethazine.
note: Search summary of NHS antihistamines page named cinnarizine and promethazine alongside chlorphenamine; page attribution inferred from summary.

sentence: The Cambridge leaflet says every antihistamine can cause some drowsiness, though it is much more likely with a sedating one.
note: As above.

sentence: The NHS says cetirizine is less likely to cause sleepiness than sedating antihistamines such as chlorphenamine, but more likely to do so than loratadine, desloratadine or fexofenadine.
note: Search summary of NHS cetirizine/antihistamines pages said these comparisons; individual page attribution not confirmed.

sentence: For cetirizine, the NHS lists feeling sleepy and tired as the most common side effect.
note: NHS: feeling sleepy and tired is the most common side effect.

sentence: Headaches, dry mouth, feeling sick, dizziness and diarrhoea are also listed.
note: NHS side effects of cetirizine listed these.

sentence: The NHS adds that some people find cetirizine sedating even though it is classed as non-drowsy.
note: Search summary: some people still find it sedating even though classed non-drowsy.

sentence: For chlorphenamine, the NHS lists drowsiness during the day, feeling sick, dizziness or trouble concentrating, dry mouth, headaches and blurred vision.
note: NHS chlorphenamine side effects common list.

sentence: It says children and people over 65 are more likely to have some side effects, such as feeling restless or excited.
note: NHS: children and over 65s more chance of some side effects such as restless or excited.

sentence: The NHS advises contacting a doctor or NHS 111 about yellowing of the skin or eyes, unusual bruising or bleeding, or difficulty passing urine while using chlorphenamine.
note: NHS: contact doctor or NHS 111 for these. The search summary also said to stop the medicine; that part is left out because it was not confirmed on the page excerpt.

sentence: A pharmacist or GP can answer non-urgent questions about side effects.
note: NHS chlorphenamine page recommends speaking to a pharmacist or GP for personal advice (search summary).

sentence: For cetirizine, the NHS says not to drive or ride a bike if it makes a person sleepy.
note: NHS: advises not to drive or ride a bike if it makes you sleepy; ask doctor or pharmacist if unsure. Reported via search summary.

sentence: If someone is unsure, the NHS says to ask a doctor or pharmacist.
note: As above.

sentence: The NHS also says it is best not to drink alcohol while taking cetirizine, because it can add to sleepiness.
note: NHS: best not to drink alcohol, can make you feel sleepy.

sentence: The Cambridge leaflet makes the same point, saying that tablets such as cetirizine can enhance the effects of alcohol.
note: CUH: antihistamine tablets such as cetirizine can enhance the effects of alcohol and cause drowsiness.

sentence: For chlorphenamine, the NHS advises not to drive or use machinery after taking it.
note: Search summary attributed this to the NHS but did not name the exact page; treat attribution as unconfirmed.

sentence: The NHS also notes that some liquid products contain a small amount of alcohol, so the packaging is worth checking.
note: Search summary of NHS who can and cannot take chlorphenamine page.

sentence: The NHS says chlorphenamine can be taken in pregnancy and that there is no good evidence it harms the baby.
note: NHS chlorphenamine pregnancy page.

sentence: It can cause drowsiness, so a doctor or pharmacist may suggest a non-drowsy antihistamine such as loratadine.
note: As above.

sentence: A summary of NHS antihistamine guidance also says loratadine is usually recommended when an antihistamine is needed in pregnancy.
note: Search summary of NHS antihistamines guidance; attribution to page inferred.

sentence: For breastfeeding, NHS guidance says loratadine or cetirizine are usually fine.
note: Search summary of NHS guidance; SPS prefers cetirizine or loratadine.

sentence: The NHS Specialist Pharmacy Service prefers non-sedating antihistamines and suggests watching the baby for drowsiness, irritability, dry mouth, poor feeding and poor weight gain.
note: SPS: prefers non-sedating, monitor infant for drowsiness, irritability, dry mouth, poor feeding, inadequate weight gain.

sentence: It says younger babies who are fed only breast milk are at greater risk of side effects.
note: SPS: younger exclusively breastfed infants at greater risk.

sentence: For chlorphenamine, the NHS says to contact NHS 111 or a healthcare professional if a breastfed baby feeds poorly or seems unusually sleepy or irritable.
note: NHS chlorphenamine pregnancy and breastfeeding page, via search summary.

sentence: For children, the NHS says most adults and children aged 1 year or over can take chlorphenamine, but it is not suitable for everyone.
note: NHS who can and cannot take chlorphenamine: most adults and children aged 1 and over can take; cautions listed.

sentence: It lists extra care for people with conditions such as glaucoma, epilepsy, asthma, heart disease, an enlarged prostate, or liver or kidney problems.
note: NHS cautions listed: angle-closure glaucoma, epilepsy, asthma/breathing problems, heart disease, enlarged prostate, liver or kidney problems, frail older adults.

sentence: One NHS formulary summary notes that age limits differ between products, so a pharmacist can help with what suits a child.
note: Search summary of South and West Devon formulary: age limits vary by product. The pharmacist route is the site's signposting.

sentence: For everyday questions, such as which antihistamine suits a person or how a side effect is behaving, a pharmacist or GP is the usual route.
note: NHS chlorphenamine pages point to a pharmacist or GP for personal advice (search summary). Signposting wording is the site's own.

sentence: NHS 111 can give urgent advice, for example about the symptoms listed above or a breastfed baby who is unusually sleepy.
note: NHS pages name NHS 111 for these situations.

sentence: The NHS says to call 999 for signs of a serious allergic reaction.
note: NHS chlorphenamine side effects page: emergency 999 signs of serious allergic reaction.

sentence: These include swelling of the lips, mouth, throat or tongue, fast or difficult breathing, a tight throat or trouble swallowing, and blue, grey or pale lips or skin.
note: NHS list.

sentence: They also include sudden confusion or extreme drowsiness, and fainting without recovery.
note: NHS list.

sentence: In children, a limp or unresponsive state is another warning sign.
note: NHS list.

sentence: The NHS also says to call 999 or go to A&E for signs of taking too much, such as a racing or irregular heartbeat, seizures or hallucinations.
note: NHS overdose signs via search summary.
